offence_severity: Imprisonment for one year under s. 498-A and three years under s. 306
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declarations of the deceased, along with the evidence of her father, were accepted by the court as sufficient to establish that the appellant used to fight on petty issues and give beatings to the deceased, which drove her to commit suicide.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the medical experts and the police officers who recorded the dying declarations, finding their testimony consistent with the ocular evidence that the deceased was in a fit condition to speak at the time of recording her statements.
trial_duration: Offence: 26.02.1991; Trial judgment: 31.08.1992; High Court decision: 16.09.2004; Supreme Court decision: 31.10.2013
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: S.S. Upadhyay, Kunwar C.M. Khan, Kurnud L. Das, Irshad Ahmad; Counsel for the State: Vikas Sharma, Kamal Mohan Gupta

appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeal in part, convicted under Sections 498A and 306, IPC

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased's dying declarations, along with the evidence of her father, establish that the appellant subjected her to cruelty and harassment, which drove her to commit suicide. They also contended that the medical experts' opinions do not contradict the ocular evidence that the deceased was fit to make her statements.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the deceased was not in a medical condition to speak due to the charred larynx and trachea, and therefore, the dying declarations should not be relied upon. They also claimed that the prosecution failed to establish that the cruelty was connected to dowry demands, which is a necessary ingredient for dowry death under Section 304-8, IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that for an offence of dowry death under Section 304-8, IPC, the prosecution must prove that the accused subjected the woman to cruelty in connection with dowry demands soon before her death. The Court also relied on the presumption under Section 113-A of the Evidence Act for abetment of suicide.
precedent_relied_upon: Bansi Lal v. State of Haryana 2011 (1) SCR 724; Smt. Shanti and Another v. State of Haryana 1990 (2) Suppl. SCR 675; K. Prema S. Rao and Another etc. v. Yadla Srinivasa Rao and Others, etc. 2002 (3) Suppl. SCR 339; Sanjiv Kumar v. State of Punjab (2009) 16 SCC 487; Durga Prasad & Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh 2010 (7) SCR 104; Gurdeep Singh v. State of Punjab & Ors. 2011 (10) SCR 655; Devinder alias Kala Ram & Ors. v. State of Haryana (2012) 10 SCC 763
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed considering the particular conduct of the appellant which drove the deceased to commit suicide, and to punish the appellant for the offences under Sections 498A and 306, IPC.
other_sentence_order: The Court imposed a sentence of one year imprisonment and fine of Rs.1,000/- for the offence under Section 498A, IPC and a sentence of three years imprisonment and fine of Rs.2,000/- for the offence under Section 306, IPC, with the sentences running concurrently. In case of failure to pay the fine, the appellant shall undergo further imprisonment for six months.
